```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
```
# Problem 1

```{r}
data("ny_noaa")
```
The NOAA New York weather dataset contains daily meteorological records across multiple weather stations in New York from 1981 to 2010.
The dataset has approximately 2595176 rows (daily observations) and 7 initial columns: `id`, `date`, `prcp`, `snow`, `snwd`, `tmax`, `tmin`.

Missing values are important in this dataset. Many rows contain NA values for temperature and snow/precipitation measurements, meaning some daily records lack valid readings. In `tmax`and `tmin`, over 40 percent of the record is missing which may affect the related plots.

## `1.1`

```{r}
ny_noaa_df = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year  = factor(year(date)),   
    month = month(date),  
    day   = mday(date),
    prcp = prcp / 10,       
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10, 
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  ) 

dim(ny_noaa_df)
summary(ny_noaa_df)

ny_noaa_df |>
  count(snow) |>
  head(10)
```

We split `date` into `year`, `month`, and `day` for future analysis. Among the variables, units of `prcp`, `tmax`, `tmin` need to be divided by 10 because their units are tenth of the reasonable units.

For snow value count, the majority of daily observations have `snow = 0`, meaning no snowfall on those days. We also observe an negative value of snowfall (`snow = -13`) which represents an erroneous data entry and it should be excluded from subsequent analysis.

## `1.2`

```{r}
mean_tmax = ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c(1,7), labels = c("January", "July"))
  ) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) 
```

```{r}
mean_tmax |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, colour = month)) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = month), se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    breaks = seq(1980, 2010, by = 5)
  ) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  labs(
    title = "Average Max Temperature Trend in January and July ", 
    x = "Year", 
    y = "Max Temp",
    caption = "Average Max Temperature in January and in July in Each Station Across Years",
    color = "Month"
  ) 
```

This two-panel figure presents boxplots of average maximum temperature for January and July, grouped by year, with smoothed trend lines overlaid.

July maximum temperatures are consistently much warmer than January maximum temperatures. Temperatures fluctuate from year to year. January shows periodic warmer and colder periods over time, while July temperatures remain relatively stable and warm across decades.

Outliers are present in both months. January has many warm high-value outliers. July also a few low-value outliers, including an unusually cold observation in 1988, representing rare anomalous weather events.

## `1.3`

```{r}
plot_1 = ny_noaa_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) + 
  geom_hex() +
  theme(legend.position = "right") + 
  labs(
    title = "Max Tem vs Min Tem", 
    x = "Minimum temperature", 
    y = "Maximum temperature"
  ) 
  


plot_2 = ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges() +
  scale_y_discrete(
    breaks = seq(1980, 2010, by = 5)
  ) +
  labs(x ="Snowfall (mm)", y =  "Year", title = "Snowfall by year") 

plot_1 + plot_2

```

This two-panel figure contains a hexbin (left) and a ridge plot (right).

The left hexbin plot illustrates the positive correlation between minimum and maximum temperatures, where higher minimums generally align with higher maximums. The color gradient highlights data density, showing that most observations are heavily concentrated in the mild temperature range (min temp between 0°C and 20°C, max temp between 0°C and 30°C), while rare extreme values outliers still exist.

The right ridgeline plot illustrates the probability density distribution of annual snowfall. Across the decades, the snowfall data exhibits a strikingly consistent multimodal distribution, characterized by distinct primary peaks at approximately 10 mm and 20–30 mm, alongside smaller secondary peaks near 50 mm and 75 mm. The temporal stability of these density profiles indicates that the regional snowfall regime is relatively stable over time.


# Problem 2

## Tidy data

```{r}
accel_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")|>
  janitor::clean_names()
covar_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv",skip = 4,
           na = c("", "NA", "."))|>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_df = 
  inner_join(
    covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn") |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education)|>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1,2), labels = c("male", "female")),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1,2,3),
      labels = c("Less than high school",
                 "High school equivalent",
                 "More than high school"),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )
```

First, we import the datasets and use `janitor::clean_names` to standardize the variable names, for `covar_df`, first 4 rows are skipped as it is descriptive content. Then we combine 2 datasets by `seqn` and exclude 22 participants less than 21 years of ages and those with missing demographic data. Variables `sex` and `education` are encoded to factors (ordered factors for `education`).

## Table

```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
    )


nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Count",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

The table shows sample size imbalance across education groups where nearly equal sexes for less-than-high-school, more males for high school equivalent and slightly more females in the highest education group.

The density plots reveal clear age differences by education level. Participants with lower educational attainment tend to be older while those with more than high school education level tend yo be younger, especially in female participants. Within each education panel, male and female age distributions differ, especially in the high school equivalent and more-than-high-school categories. The high school equivalent group contains a substantial number of younger males, creating an earlier peak in the male age distribution. In more-than-high-school category, female group has higher peak between 20 and 40 than male group.

## Total activities

```{r}

nhanes_df |>
  rowwise() |>  
  mutate(
    total_act = sum(c_across(min1:min1440))
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_act, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity vs Age by Education and Sex",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Total Daily MIMS Activity",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

These scatter plots display the relationship between total daily MIMS activity and age, separated by education level and colored by sex. Across all 3 education groups, total daily physical activity generally declines with increasing age.

Sex differences in activity levels vary across educational backgrounds. For individuals with a high school education or higher, females consistently maintain higher average MIMS activity levels than males across almost all age groups. While in the 'Less than high school' group, males and females show similar levels during early adulthood and among participants older than 40, males have higher activity levels than females.

Education appears to buffer against early-age activity decline. Participants in the 'More than high school' category display a relatively plateaued activity level between ages 20 and 60 for both males and females. In contrast, those with 'Less than high school' or 'High school equivalent' education demonstrate earlier peaks and sharper drops in activity.

## 3 panel plot

```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "MIMS"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.integer(str_remove(minute, "min")),
    hour = minute / 60
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = MIMS, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "24 hour Activity Time Course by Education Level",
    x = "Hour of Day (0~24)",
    y = "Average MIMS Value",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

This figure shows loess-smoothed curves of minute-level MIMS activity values over the 24-hour day, faceted by education level and colored by sex. Across all education levels, activity is lowest during sleep (before 5 AM) and increases up rapidly starting at 5 AM as people wake up and begin their day.

Women generally show higher activity levels during the day than men in most groups. For people with a high school equivalent or higher education, women maintain noticeably higher activity values from morning until evening. However, in the 'Less than high school' group, men and women follow almost identical daytime patterns, with women only showing a slightly higher peak around noon.

Educational background changes how daytime activity is distributed. People with less than high school education have a single sharp peak around midday followed by a steady drop in the afternoon. In contrast, those with higher education maintain a steady, high-level plateau of activity throughout normal working hours (from 10 AM to 6 PM).

# Problem 3
